entries.text: Spanish for "pressed". Herbal cannabis compressed into hard blocks for transport, typical of the cannabis grown in Paraguay and sold across South America.
A North African name for hashish, used in Morocco and in the colonial drug laws of France and Belgium.
Still against the law, but no longer a crime. Having a small amount brings at most a fine or a warning, and no criminal record.
Still a crime on paper, but in practice no punishment is imposed for small amounts.
Illegal, but the authorities have decided not to prosecute, as with the Dutch coffeeshops.
A breach handled by an authority instead of a criminal court, usually with a fine and no criminal record.
A minor crime, below a felony. It can bring a short jail term and leaves a criminal record.
A serious crime, usually one that can bring more than a year in prison.
In drug law, supplying drugs to anyone else, sold or given away, not only smuggling them across borders.
A rule that treats anyone holding more than a set amount as a dealer, unless they prove otherwise.
A prison term the judge must impose at least, whatever the circumstances of the case.
Corporal punishment with a rattan cane, still imposed for drug crimes in Singapore and Malaysia.
An on-the-spot fine, like a parking ticket, paid without going to court.
Sending someone to treatment, education or a warning instead of to court.
Removing an old conviction from a person's criminal record.
The United Nations treaty of 1961 that obliges countries to control cannabis and to limit it to medical and scientific use.

The strictest classes in a drug law's lists. Schedule I in the United States is for drugs said to have no accepted medical use; Schedule IV of the 1961 UN treaty was for drugs considered especially dangerous.
Tetrahydrocannabinol, the main substance in cannabis that makes people high.
Hexahydrocannabinol, a semi-synthetic cannabinoid usually made from CBD and sold as a legal high, until many countries banned it.
A substance that acts on the body's cannabinoid receptors, such as THC or CBD.
A cannabinoid the body makes itself, such as anandamide.
A driving rule under which a set level of THC in the blood is an offence by itself, whether or not the driver is impaired.
Nanograms per millilitre, the unit for THC in blood or serum. A nanogram is a billionth of a gram.
Food or sweets made with cannabis, such as cookies, chocolate or gummies.
Strong extracts of cannabis, such as oil, wax or shatter, with far more THC than the flower.
A non-profit club whose members grow cannabis together and share the harvest only among themselves.
A legal market in which the state licenses growers and sellers and sets rules on products, prices or buyers.
Growing a few cannabis plants at home for one's own use, legal in some countries within a set number of plants.
Doctors' consultations held online, through which some countries' patients get cannabis prescriptions without a visit.
The United Nations treaty of 1971 that controls psychotropic substances, among them THC itself; the cannabis plant is controlled by the treaty of 1961.
The United Nations treaty of 1988 against drug trafficking. It also asks countries to make possession for personal use a criminal offence, within the limits of their constitutions.

also: UN Office on Drugs and Crime
United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime
entries.text: The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, which collects countries' drug figures and publishes the yearly World Drug Report.
The UN body that watches whether countries keep the drug treaties, and criticises those that legalise cannabis.
The UN commission where governments vote on which substances the drug treaties control. In 2020 it took cannabis out of the treaty's strictest list.
The European Union Drugs Agency in Lisbon, called the EMCDDA until 2024, which gathers drug figures from the EU countries.
Moving a drug to another list of a drug law or treaty, which changes how strictly it is controlled.
Holding or using drugs for oneself rather than to supply anyone else. Many laws punish it far more lightly than dealing.
An offence treated as more serious because of its circumstances, such as selling to children, near a school or as part of a gang, which raises the punishment.
A prison term the court imposes but does not enforce, unless the person offends again within a set period.
A sentence served in the community under supervision instead of in prison, with conditions such as regular drug tests.
A fine counted in days, each day worth a share of the person's income, so the same offence costs the rich more. Used in Germany and the Nordic countries.
A decision that frees people from punishment for past offences or clears their convictions, usually after a law has changed.
A driving rule under which any trace of THC in the body is an offence, however long ago the cannabis was used.
Equipment for using drugs, such as pipes, bongs, papers and grinders. Some laws make selling or holding it an offence.
Drug treatment ordered by a court or the authorities, sometimes in a closed rehabilitation centre, that the person cannot refuse.
In Portugal, a panel of health and social workers to which the police send people caught with drugs for their own use, instead of to a court.
In Russia and other former Soviet states, an official list of people known to use drugs, which can cost them a driving licence and some jobs.
Measures that reduce the damage drug use does, such as drug checking or advice on safer use, without first requiring people to stop.
A mouth spray made from cannabis extracts, with THC and CBD in roughly equal parts, approved in many countries for muscle stiffness in multiple sclerosis. Its generic name is nabiximols.
THC made as a medicine, mainly against nausea and loss of appetite.
A man-made substance similar to THC, prescribed against nausea during chemotherapy.
A medicine made up by a pharmacist for one patient from a doctor's prescription, such as a cannabis oil dosed for that person.
The acid form of THC found in the raw plant. It does not make people high until it is heated, which some sellers use to sell strong flower as "hemp".
Laboratory chemicals that act like THC, often far stronger and more dangerous, sold under names such as Spice or K2.
A strong liquid extract of cannabis, with much more THC than the flower or hashish.
How strong a cannabis product is, usually given as its share of THC.
A tax on a particular product, such as alcohol, tobacco or legal cannabis, charged on top of ordinary sales tax.
Destroying cannabis crops, by hand, by burning or by spraying from the air, usually by police or soldiers.
Taking a person into official custody over a suspected offence. An arrest does not itself mean that the person has been charged or found guilty.
A formal accusation that someone committed an offence. A charge still has to be proved; it is not a conviction.
Being held under the control of the authorities, for example in a police station or prison. Custody can come before trial as well as after conviction.
A person the authorities believe may have been involved in an offence. This describes a stage of an investigation, not a finding of guilt.
The person or other party a legal case is brought against. In a criminal report, calling someone a defendant does not itself mean the court has found them guilty.
Bringing and pursuing a criminal case against someone. The word can also mean the side presenting the case against the accused.
The lawyer or official who presents the criminal case against the accused on behalf of the prosecuting authority.
A formal written accusation used in some criminal proceedings. Who issues it and how it is approved vary between legal systems; it does not establish guilt.
A person's formal admission in court that they committed the offence charged. It is different from being found guilty after a contested trial.
A court's formal finding that a person is guilty of an offence, following a guilty plea or a trial. It is a later stage than arrest or charge.
A court's finding that the accused is not guilty of the charge. It is different from releasing someone while the case continues.
Asking a higher court to review a decision, such as a conviction or sentence. The higher court may uphold or change that decision.
In custody reports, holding an accused person while they await trial or sentencing. In other court contexts, remand can instead mean sending a case back to a lower court.
Release from custody while a case continues, usually with conditions such as returning to court. Some systems require money or a guarantee, but bail does not always involve a payment.
Sentences served at the same time rather than added together. Two fully concurrent terms of five years and three years take five years to serve, before any release rules apply.
Sentences served one after another. Terms of five years and three years served consecutively add up to eight years, before any release rules apply.
Conditional release from prison before the full sentence has been served. The person remains subject to conditions and may be returned to prison if they break them.
A prison sentence expressed as life rather than a fixed number of years. Whether release is possible depends on the law and the particular sentence.
An order authorising officials to search a specified place for evidence. It is an investigative power, not a finding that an offence has been proved.
A legal process in which one country surrenders a person to another for prosecution or to serve a criminal sentence. It is different from deporting someone under immigration law.
Authorities taking control of drugs, money or other property under legal powers. A seizure does not by itself establish guilt or permanently transfer ownership to the state.
Loss of property to the state through a legal process, for example because it was linked to an offence. It is different from a temporary seizure during an investigation.
Authorities taking property away under legal powers. Reports may use the word for either a seizure or permanent forfeiture, so the exact legal order matters.
An investigation in which authorities allow a suspect shipment to continue under supervision so they can identify the people involved. It does not mean that the shipment has become legal.
Intercepting drugs or other prohibited goods before they reach their destination, for example at a border or along a transport route.
A batch of goods sent together as one shipment. In these reports it usually means a load of cannabis being transported.
An estimate of what drugs might sell for in the retail market. It is not a record of money actually paid, and figures based on different prices or assumptions are not directly comparable.
In drug laws and agency names, a label for controlled drugs that can include cannabis. The label is not a precise description of a substance's effects.
Affecting mental processes such as perception, thinking or mood. In a law or treaty, psychotropic substances refers to the substances covered by that particular legal list.
A chemical used in making a drug. Many precursor chemicals also have ordinary legal uses, so controls often concern preventing their diversion into illegal production.
A house or other building used to grow cannabis indoors, often with artificial lighting and climate-control equipment. The name does not establish whether it is licensed or illegal.
Growing plants without soil, with nutrients supplied in water. The word describes a growing method, not a cannabis variety or a guaranteed level of THC.
An area of 10,000 square metres, or about 2.47 acres. Crop area alone does not tell us how much dried cannabis it would produce.
A metric unit of 1,000 kilograms, about 2,205 pounds. It is different from the US short ton, which is about 907 kilograms.
One hundred thousand in the South Asian numbering system. A lakh is a number, not a currency; one lakh rupees means 100,000 rupees.
Ten million in the South Asian numbering system, equal to one hundred lakh. The currency still matters; a crore of Indian rupees is not a crore of Sri Lankan rupees.
A Thai unit of land area equal to 1,600 square metres, or 0.16 hectares. It measures land, not the amount of cannabis harvested.
The weight of plant material before drying, including its moisture. It is not directly comparable with the weight of dried cannabis.
A meeting time of five Californian schoolboys in 1971 that became the worldwide code for cannabis and the date of its yearly demonstrations.
The Russian slang word for cannabis and hashish, borrowed from Uzbek and Tajik. It names the drug of the Soviet south, and of the wild hemp of the Chuy valley.

A medieval Arabic insult for the Nizari Ismailis of Syria, ḥashīshiyya, that became the European word for a hired killer. Medieval legends of drugged killers, repeated by Marco Polo and given scholarly authority in 1809, later helped make cannabis itself an “assassin of youth”.
The Swahili word for cannabis, linked to bhang and Indian Ocean exchange. Its immediate source and route inland are less certain than a simple borrowing from Hindi suggests.
The leaves of the plant, ground to a paste and eaten or drunk. In India it is the one form of cannabis that the national law leaves alone.
The name Panama's 1935 Judicial Register gives for cannabis, "commonly known locally as Canyac or Kan Jac".

Cannabidiol, the cannabis compound that does not get people high. Studied since 1940, it became a word on shop shelves only after 2018, and the law still cannot agree whether it is a medicine, a food, a drug or none of these.
Malawi's word for cannabis, one of the country's three famous C's along with its fish and its tea.
Resin rubbed by hand from the living plant, the hashish of the Himalaya. Indian law names it in its definition of cannabis.
The southern African word, from Khoekhoe. First written down by the Dutch at the Cape in 1658, later a word of contempt, now reclaimed.

Short for delta-8-THC, a close chemical cousin of the THC in cannabis, made in bulk from legal hemp after 2018 and sold in American petrol stations as a legal high. The word names a loophole as much as a molecule, and the loophole closes in November 2026.
A Central African word for cannabis that turns up on three coasts of the Atlantic, wherever enslaved and freed Central Africans were taken.

An old word for a place that hands out medicine, which in the United States became the name of the cannabis shop. The medical word was chosen because, for twenty years, medicine was the only legal ground cannabis could be sold on.

The everyday Turkish word for cannabis means "secrets". A medieval dervish poet was already using it for the drug, and it named the hashish dens that Ottoman and Republican police spent a century trying to close.
The Hindi word for the flowering tops. Indian labourers carried it to the Caribbean, and it also became the usual word across South-East Asia.
Persian for flower, and a name for herbal cannabis whose rise in urban Iran carried ideas about class, modernity and belonging.
Arabic for dried grass. The word for cannabis resin from Morocco to Afghanistan.
The name under which the British Empire, and then the world, first brought cannabis under control. It survives in the statute books of dozens of countries that have nothing to do with India.
Two Latin names from eighteenth-century botany that became the vocabulary of the modern cannabis shop. Botanists now doubt they name different things at all.
A Rwandan name for cannabis documented in 1959–60 interviews. The record also shows how a word for a plant could carry social prejudice about its users.
From the Arabic for pleasure. In Morocco it means chopped cannabis mixed with tobacco, smoked in a long thin pipe.

Named after the Hindu Kush, the mountains whose hashish plants were carried to California in the 1970s. It became the most famous strain name in the world, and, in Sierra Leone, the name of something else entirely.

A farmers' variety, kept by saving seed in the place where it grows rather than bred to a standard. The word came from German agronomy and, in cannabis, names the old local populations of the hashish and ganja regions, many of them lost to hybrids and eradication. Morocco now licenses its own, beldiya.
The Chinese character for hemp, among the oldest recorded names for the plant. It also carries the sense of numbness.
Brazil's word for cannabis, from Kimbundu, a language of Angola. It crossed the Atlantic with enslaved people, like the plant itself.
The Sesotho word for cannabis connects generations of Basotho smallholder cultivation with South Africa’s market and Lesotho’s newer licensed medical industry.
Zimbabwe's word for a crop that has grown there for centuries. Near the Mozambican border, and across it, the name is suruma.
Mexican and Central American Spanish for marijuana since at least the end of the nineteenth century. In older Spanish it is a speck or a tuft of fluff; how it came to mean the plant is unknown.

The Mongolian word for hemp also means rope or cordage. Its compounds connect the plant with oil, textiles and livestock tethers; a proverb finds strength in a rope’s twist and in people helping one another.
A Hawaiian name for cannabis, literally “numbing tobacco.” It also appears as pakalolo in Hawaiʻi's local English and Pidgin.

The Maltese word for hemp, familiar through ropes, textiles and birdseed. Drug legislation used qanneb indjan, “Indian hemp”; Article 25 of the 2021 reform literally replaced those words with “Cannabis”.
American slang of the jazz age for a cannabis cigarette, and the word that gave its name to the most famous anti-drug film ever made.
The Malagasy name for cannabis, the fibre plant and the drug alike: a textile word that became a colonial offence and is still the everyday name on Madagascar.
Spanish for "without seed". The word for unpollinated female plants came north from Mexico in the 1970s and changed what people expected cannabis to be.
A Jamaican word of unknown origin for a cannabis cigarette. In Europe it came to mean one rolled with tobacco.
New Zealand slang for a small deal of cannabis wrapped in tinfoil, and for the "tinny house", an ordinary-looking home where it is sold to anyone with cash.
The Dutch word borrowed from English weed. It usually means herbal cannabis, while hasj means resin; the Opium Act uses the plant names hennep and cannabis.
The Creole word for cannabis on Réunion. It seems to come from Madagascar, though modern Malagasy does not use it; on the island it names a plant, a temper and a book of poems.
Tunisia's everyday word for cannabis. An older name, takrouri, is the one in the decrees of the French protectorate.
